items.followUp: Define a colloid and give one example.

rubric.why: The definition must identify the dispersed particles as insoluble and describe their settling.
rubric.description: Defines a suspension as a mixture of insoluble particles that settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature of a suspension.

rubric.why: A relevant example shows the student can identify a suspension.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which insoluble particles are dispersed in a liquid and settle on standing.

items.followUp: Why is water an important solvent in living organisms?

rubric.why: The answer should state water's unusually broad dissolving ability.
rubric.description: States that water dissolves a very large variety of substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its broad solvent ability.

rubric.why: This identifies the name given to water because of that property.
rubric.description: Links this property to the name “universal solvent.”
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming or explaining the term.

modelAnswer: Water dissolves more substances than any other liquid.
Therefore, it is called the universal solvent.

items.followUp: Define a suspension and give one example.

rubric.why: A true solution is homogeneous, with the solute uniformly mixed in the solvent.
rubric.description: Defines a true solution as a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A true solution is a homogeneous mixture in which the solute is uniformly mixed with the solvent.
Example: sodium chloride dissolved in water.

items.followUp: What is meant by weak electrolytes? Give one example.

rubric.why: Strong electrolytes produce ions completely in aqueous solution or molten state.
rubric.description: States that strong electrolytes ionize completely to form ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for complete ionization or dissociation.

rubric.why: A suitable example must be a strong electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: Strong electrolytes ionize completely into ions in aqueous solution.

items.followUp: Give two uses of potassium or another common metal.

rubric.why: Sodium is used in vapour lamps, including some street lighting.
rubric.description: Gives one valid use of sodium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct use.

rubric.why: A second distinct valid use is required.
rubric.description: Gives a second valid use of sodium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different correct use.

modelAnswer: Sodium is used in sodium-vapour lamps.
It is also used as a coolant in nuclear reactors.

items.followUp: Define electronegativity and give one example of an electropositive element.

rubric.why: Electropositive character is the tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
rubric.description: Defines electropositive character as the tendency to lose electrons and form cations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining tendency.

rubric.why: These are examples of electropositive elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: Electropositive character is the tendency of an atom to lose electrons and form a positive ion.

items.followUp: Write the chemical equation for the reaction of ethane with chlorine in sunlight.

rubric.why: The equation should show methane reacting with chlorine under light.
rubric.description: Writes the reactants and indicates the light condition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct reactants and condition.

rubric.why: The first substitution product is chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.
rubric.description: Gives the correct products in the equation.

modelAnswer: Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight by substitution.

items.followUp: Describe how the electron was discovered and state two of its properties.

rubric.why: Chadwick's experiment involved bombarding beryllium with alpha particles, supplied by a radioactive source such as polonium.
rubric.description: Describes the beryllium bombardment with alpha particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the target and bombardment.

rubric.why: The penetrating radiation knocked protons out of paraffin wax, leading to the neutron's identification.
rubric.description: Explains the evidence that led to the discovery of the neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the paraffin/proton evidence or the conclusion that the radiation was a neutron.

rubric.why: A neutron has no electric charge.
rubric.description: States that a neutron is electrically neutral.

rubric.why: A neutron has approximately the same mass as a proton, about 1 amu.
rubric.description: States the approximate mass of a neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for approximately 1 amu or approximately the proton's mass.

rubric.why: Neutrons are constituents of atomic nuclei.
rubric.description: States that neutrons are found in the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for their location in the nucleus.

modelAnswer: In 1932, James Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha particles from a polonium source.
The resulting penetrating radiation knocked protons out of paraffin wax; Chadwick concluded that the radiation consisted of neutral particles called neutrons.
A neutron has no electric charge.
Its mass is approximately 1 amu, nearly equal to the mass of a proton.
Neutrons are present in the nucleus of an atom.
